conversation.name: Incident 0078: what happened, in order

place: Incident 0078: what happened, in order
title: Incident 0078: what happened, in order
text:
Longer than Wren's note because the interesting part is not the timeline.

The limiter did exactly what it is built to do. It refused about a third of nine thousand requests a minute, correctly, with the right headers. The failure is that refusing is not cheap: every 429 reads a counter in Redis and resolves the org in Postgres, so a client that retries into a closed door consumes the same backend capacity as one being served. One customer's retry loop therefore spends everybody else's capacity, and nothing about that is specific to Northwind. Any client with a fixed retry timer does it.

The second-order effect is the one I want people to notice. The scheduler's share table refreshes over the same infrastructure, so it went stale at 20:21 and placement fell back to plain FIFO for 26 minutes. We spent March building a queue that does not do head-of-line blocking and on Tuesday evening we were running the old one. We only know that because the staleness gauge exists, and the gauge exists because Oskar refused to approve the change without it.

The process finding is simpler and worse. Northwind told us the window was moving, twice, a week apart. I read the mail. Nothing happened. There is also an issue from the second of April asking whether their client backs off, which nobody answered for ten weeks.

Two changes today: shed a persistent offender from memory before touching anything, and cap how deep one org can queue. Neither is the real answer, which is a concurrency contract, and that is a conversation not a pull request.

text:
As promised, an update whether or not I had a cause. I do not have a cause.

What we know. Six reports since Tuesday, from two customers, so this is not specific to your pipeline. Four cache keys in our last 2,100 uploads have held two different artifacts at different times. All four were written in the last nine days.

What we have ruled out, and how. A partially written upload cannot be read back under the key, so these are two complete writes rather than one corrupted one. A single machine producing different output each run is out too: forty rebuilds of 8f21c4 on our side came out byte identical.

What we changed this week. Every cache write now records the full set of inputs its key was derived from. Artifacts are held for seven days after eviction instead of being deleted, and our cache upload logs went from three days to fourteen. None of that fixes anything; it means the next occurrence can be diagnosed in an hour rather than four days.

Your decision to take release builds off the cache is the one I would have made. Next update Tuesday, or sooner if we find it.

conversation.name: Session pooling, before the review

place: Session pooling, before the review
title: Session pooling, before the review
text:
Writing this now so that at one o'clock we are arguing about a position rather than discovering one.

I think we should use session pooling, and I think the case for it is weaker than I would like, so here is both halves.

For: under session mode a client holds its server connection for the life of the connection, which means every semantic our four services were written against still holds. Advisory locks, prepared statements, temp tables, LISTEN. Nothing in the scheduler changes, nothing in the api changes, and the version upgrade on Thursday is then genuinely the only change in flight. I have a strong preference for one change at a time four weeks after an incident caused by two.

Against, and this is the part I cannot get around: session mode does not reduce the number of backends unless clients wait. It converts a memory problem into a queueing problem. If the scheduler waits for a server connection, dispatch waits, and dispatch waiting is what August was - not for the same reason, but it looks the same on the graph and it produces the same phone call.

So I will make the argument and I expect to lose it. What I want out of the hour is that the scheduler's four session dependencies are named in the document and that the temp table is written down as unsolved rather than as a follow-up. A follow-up is a thing people assume is nearly done.

Autovacuum has never been tuned on it and the table is append-only, so the default settings have been doing nothing useful for two years.

conversation.name: Postgres 17: the case, the risks, and no date

place: Postgres 17: the case, the risks, and no date
title: Postgres 17: the case, the risks, and no date
text:
Ahead of eleven o'clock.

The case is dull: we run 14.12, community support ends in November 2026, and after that a security fix means an emergency upgrade rather than a planned one. That is the whole argument. Nothing in 15, 16 or 17 is a feature we need, though the 17 changes to vacuum and to logical replication are both in our favour.

The risks, in the order I am worried about them. Connections: we sit at roughly 340 of 400 and the scheduler holds 80 of those. The class is declared next to the route in the same list that says the route is audited at all, so a new route with no declaration fails to compile rather than silently becoming operational.

Also decided: read access is a role. Inside a customer's org their owner grants it and the grant is itself an audit entry. On our side it is break-glass with a reason and an eight hour expiry, and the production console goes through the same check, which ends the nine accounts that exist by convention.

And: the first partition drop is run by a person in a window. No cron this quarter.

The argument worth keeping is Liesl's - whether having a deletion schedule at all reads badly to an auditor. The estimated part. Cold start lands around 11 seconds: the image is resident, so a claim is a container start rather than an install. Worse than the 9.4 the pool gives the 79% who hit it, much better than the 38 the rest pay, and there is no idle fleet underneath it.

The part I do not know. Drift. A nightly bake makes a subtly different machine every night, and the failure mode is a build that worked yesterday failing today with nothing changed by anyone. We have had that exact shape before, in April, with the cache key. Pinned versions and the image digest in the build record are the two things I would want before this goes near a customer.

title: Postgres 17: the plan, and what I need from each of you
text:
Two changes, and everyone keeps saying them as one.

The version. 14 to 17, pg_upgrade --link, four minutes of read-only. Staging this Thursday at 07:30. Production is not scheduled and I am not scheduling it this week.

The pooler. This is the one with behaviour in it. We hold 1,180 backend connections at peak and about 900 of them are idle at any given moment; each one costs roughly nine megabytes and a slot. pgbouncer in transaction mode takes that to under a hundred. In transaction mode a client gets a server connection for the length of a transaction and not one moment longer, which means anything that depends on a connection remembering something between two statements stops working. Silently, in most cases.

What I need by Tuesday morning, in kiln/infra#94 and not in a reply to this: every place your service depends on session state. Advisory locks, prepared statements, temp tables, cursors held across transactions, LISTEN/NOTIFY, SET of anything. If you are not sure whether something counts, put it in the list and I will say.

text:
Between 7 and 15 April, some builds on Kiln were served cached compiler output produced by a different version of the Go toolchain than the one the build requested. The cache key we use to decide whether a previous build's output can be reused did not include the toolchain, so two builds that differed only by compiler version were treated as the same build.

We found this on the evening of 14 April after two customer reports, declared an incident at 21:40 CEST, and cleared the entire build cache. That completed at 01:05 on 15 April. Any build started after that time cannot be affected.

We have sent affected customers the list of their build ids that fall in the window. We are changing the cache key to include the toolchain and the exact image digest; that work is in progress and we will confirm when it ships. Builds will be slower than usual for the rest of this week while the cache refills.

Faye Okonjo, Support Engineering

title: The hit rate, and why
text:
Writing this up properly while it is fresh, because in three months the graph will just look like a step and nobody will remember what caused it.

At 14:20 the hit rate went from 84% to 31% in about six minutes. Not a slope. The only component that differs between the misses and the entries we already had is the toolchain: go1.24.3 in the old keys, go1.24.5 in everything after 14:18.

That is working as designed. kiln/cache#103 put the toolchain in the key in April precisely so that a build made with a different compiler cannot be served an artifact made with another one. What we did not have was any way to see it, which is why I spent Monday adding a per-toolchain breakdown - two days before we needed it, by luck rather than foresight.

The refill is roughly nine thousand distinct keys a day across the repositories that matter. Most of it lands Friday, the long tail over the weekend. I do not think there is anything to do except watch it and not panic.

The thing I would change is upstream of the cache. If the image is allowed to move the toolchain without anyone deciding to, then every image bake is a cache flush, and eventually one of those happens on a Monday morning at the same time as something else and it is an incident instead of an afternoon.

conversation.name: ADR-0026: prebaked images replace the warm pool

place: ADR-0026: prebaked images replace the warm pool
title: ADR-0026: prebaked images replace the warm pool
text:
I have written this one rather than asking Marin to, because ADR-0022 is mine and the person who reverses a decision should be the person who made it.

The short version. The warm pool does what it said it would - cold start went from 38.1 seconds to 9.4 and has stayed there. What it did not do is cost what I said it would. Sixteen machines resident across four availability zones is 7,180 EUR in July against an estimate of 2,050, and the gap is entirely that I assumed the pool drains during the day. It does not, because the refill loop puts the machines straight back.

What replaces it is one base image per region, baked nightly from a toolchain manifest, with the launch template reading the image id. Expected cold start is between ten and thirteen seconds. That is worse than the pool and roughly a tenth of the price.

The part I would like read properly is the rollback, because it is the thing that made me nervous about images in May. Previous AMI id stays in SSM and the ASG pins a template version, so going back is one apply and no bake.

place: Metering: what I am actually rewriting, and why it is three weeks
title: Metering: what I am actually rewriting, and why it is three weeks
text:
Before anyone asks me for a date again, here is the shape of it.

A build minute is computed in three places. The usage API sums durations from the raw build rows. The invoice renderer sums the daily rollup table. The dashboard calls the API and caches for an hour. Those are three numbers with one name, and two of them round, at different points, for different reasons.

None of that is a bug on its own. The rollup exists because summing four months of raw rows for every dashboard load was killing the primary in 2024, and rounding in it was a deliberate decision by somebody who is no longer here. The API rounds at the end because that is where money is named. Each of those choices is defensible in the file it lives in.

The rewrite is one path. The rollup becomes a cache of a query rather than a source of truth, the rate table gets versions and validity windows so that regenerating an invoice twice gives the same answer twice, and every figure we show carries which of those it came from.

Three weeks. Four if the backfill has to reconcile against invoices we have already sent, and I think it does, because the moment the new number differs from a sent invoice by a cent somebody has to decide what we do about that and it will not be me.

The control the auditor will test is that every privileged action against a customer's builds is attributable to a person or a token. Once Marin's change is in, the three build routes satisfy that from the date it merges. Everything before that date does not, and there is no honest way to make it, because the data was never written.

So we declare it. One dated sentence in the evidence pack saying coverage begins on 9 July 2026 and why. Auditors see declared gaps constantly. What they do not see often is a company that found its own, and that is worth more to us than a tidier answer would be.

Two things are still unowned and I want to say so while there is time. There is no retention policy for the audit log - not a short one, not a long one, none - and there is no documented access path for who may read it. Both need a decision before the evidence window closes. Neither is urgent this month and both will be urgent in a month I am not planning for.

I have filed it separately so it is somebody's rather than nobody's.

Volume. 182,000 rows a day. The table is 61 GB and fourteen months old and has never been pruned, because there is no policy to prune it by and nobody has hit a disk alarm yet.

Reads. Nothing. Not stored, not sampled, not counted. builds and orgs served 14.2 million GETs yesterday and we cannot tell you whether any of them was a person reading an org they had no business in.

Access. The read route is behind org admin, which is fine. The table is behind production database access, which is twelve accounts, which is the same twelve from your March review - four of them mine, three service accounts from the January shard migration and one personal read-only. I said I would decide about those by the end of that week and I did not, and I am telling you that rather than letting you find it.

The part I think is genuinely worth doing is reads, and not all of them. A control cares about somebody reading the audit log, the member list, the token list, or an artefact. It does not care about a build polling its own status four times a minute, and if we log that we will have built a very expensive way to store nothing.

title: SOC 2 Type II: what the hour at eleven is for
text:
Read this before rather than during, and then the hour is enough.

Type II is not the one where somebody checks the controls exist on a Tuesday. It is the one where they check the controls operated over a window, and the window is nine months. So anything we fix in August is a control that operated for four months, and anything we do not fix is an exception in a report that Northwind's security team will read.

140 questions in the questionnaire. Roughly ninety are documents - a policy that exists, or a policy that takes an afternoon to write honestly. Thirty are process and they belong to me and Bruno. Twenty are engineering, and seventeen of those are already true and only need evidence: reviews on pull requests, encryption at rest, backups, quarterly access review.

The three that are not true are all the audit log in kiln/api, and they are the whole reason this is an engineering conversation rather than a paperwork one.

title: Kickoff notes, and what we owe you by Thursday
text:
Thanks both. Writing down what we agreed so there is one version of it.

The pilot is two repositories for six weeks from Thursday 2 April. Your peak across the whole estate is twelve thousand builds a day, of which the pilot repositories are roughly a fifth, and most of that arrives in the nightly backfill between 01:00 and 04:00 your time.

What we owe you: credentials today, a webhook signature verification example in Go with test fixtures before Wednesday, and a shared Slack channel which is open now. Marin has the webhook piece.

What we would like from you: a heads-up before the first night you run the full backfill through us, so somebody is watching rather than finding out in the morning.

Support is the shared channel during working hours, Berlin time. Out of hours it reaches whoever is holding the pager. Please do use it - we would much rather hear something is slow on the day than read about it in a summary in six weeks.

conversation.name: Halversen invoice: GBP total is a cent under the lines

place: Halversen invoice: GBP total is a cent under the lines
title: Halversen invoice: GBP total is a cent under the lines
text:
Forwarding this before it grows. Halversen are on SUP-4412. They bill in GBP against a EUR contract, and their February invoice reads GBP 1,284.16 while the line items on the same invoice add up to GBP 1,284.17.

It is a penny. They have gone back through November, December and January and it is a penny every time, always in their favour, which they have pointed out themselves and which I think tells you what kind of team they are. Their words: 'we are not asking for a cent, we are asking which number is the one we should be reconciling against'.

That is a fair question and I do not know the answer. If the total is the truth then the lines are decoration, and the lines are what their finance team pastes into a spreadsheet.

Dmitri, I have filed it. No rush from their side - they have asked for an answer this month, not this week.
